archetypes.title: Scrap Mix Optimization
archetypes.operatorDescription: Every heat starts with the charge bucket, and if you get the mix wrong, you're chasing chemistry the rest of the way through the melt shop and the ladle. The melt foreman has maybe eight to fifteen scrap grades sitting in the yard - busheling, #1 HMS, shredded, turnings, plate and structural, obsolete grades - all at different prices, different densities, different residual profiles. The job is to fill two or three charge buckets that hit the target weight, fit inside the furnace volume, keep copper and tin and chromium residuals under the grade ceiling, and do it at the lowest possible scrap cost per ton of liquid steel.

archetypes.title: Scrap Yard Logistics
archetypes.operatorDescription: The scrap yard is the most chaotic part of any melt shop operation. You have got two or three overhead cranes working the yard, trucks coming in to dump loads, a charge car that needs buckets filled and staged at the furnace on time, and a yard layout that changes every shift depending on what got delivered and what got consumed. If the crane is not in position when the furnace needs the next bucket, you are adding dead time to the tap-to-tap cycle, and that is real money - every minute of delay on a furnace running 40-50 heats a day costs throughput.

You buy #1 HMS and the cert says 0.10% copper max, but what actually shows up on the truck can run 0.08 to 0.22% depending on the source region, the time of year, and frankly how honest the dealer is. Shredded scrap is even worse because it is a mixed stream - cars, appliances, whatever went into the shredder that day.

archetypes.title: DRI/HBI Blending Optimization
archetypes.operatorDescription: Mills that run direct reduced iron - whether DRI or its briquetted cousin HBI - have a different game than pure scrap shops. DRI gives you virgin iron with almost zero residuals, which is gold when you are making low-copper automotive grades. archetypes.title: Electrical Energy Optimization
archetypes.operatorDescription: The EAF is the single biggest electricity consumer in a mini-mill, and the power profile you run determines everything - melt rate, electrode consumption, refractory wear, noise, flicker, and of course the electric bill. The furnace guys have a standard power curve: you start on a lower tap after charging (boring-in through the scrap pile), ramp up to max power once you have a flat bath, and then back off toward the end when you are refining temperature. But "standard" does not mean "optimal." Every heat is different - the scrap mix, the charge weight, the arc length stability, the panel cooling water temperature, the electricity price at that hour.

archetypes.title: Electrode Consumption Management
archetypes.operatorDescription: Graphite electrodes are one of the most expensive consumables in the melt shop. At $3,000-5,000 per ton for UHP-grade graphite, and consumption running 1.2-1.8 kg per ton of steel, you are looking at $4-9 per ton of liquid steel just for electrodes. On a million-ton shop, that is $4M-9M a year.

archetypes.title: Oxygen/Carbon Injection Profile Optimization
archetypes.operatorDescription: Oxygen and carbon injection in the EAF is where the chemistry really gets made. You are blowing oxygen through door lances, wall-mounted injectors, or a combination - maybe 30-50 Nm3/ton of O2 per heat on a modern shop. The oxygen does multiple jobs: it cuts scrap during meltdown, it decarburizes the bath, it generates chemical energy (oxidizing carbon and iron generates heat that supplements the electrical input), and it helps form a foamy slag when combined with carbon injection.

archetypes.title: Flux Addition Optimization
archetypes.operatorDescription: Slag is the unsung hero of steelmaking - get it right and the furnace runs smooth, the steel is clean, and the refractory lasts. Get it wrong and you are fighting the furnace all day. The main fluxes are burnt lime (CaO) and dolomite (MgO-CaO), and the job is to hit a target slag basicity (CaO/SiO2 ratio, typically 1.8-2.5 for EAF operations) while maintaining enough MgO to saturate the slag and protect the refractory lining.

archetypes.title: Slag Foaming Optimization
archetypes.operatorDescription: A good foamy slag is the single biggest lever for EAF energy efficiency after the power profile itself. When the slag foams up and buries the arc, two things happen: the arc energy transfers into the bath through the slag blanket instead of radiating directly onto the sidewall and roof panels, and the furnace noise drops dramatically (the neighbors appreciate that too). A well-foamed slag can reduce energy consumption by 20-30 kWh/ton and cut electrode sidewall oxidation by 30-50%.

archetypes.title: Slag Chemistry Optimization
archetypes.operatorDescription: BOF slag is not just a waste product that you dump in the slag pit - it is an active refining tool that determines phosphorus removal, sulfur capacity, iron yield, and vessel lining life. archetypes.title: BOF Gas Recovery Optimization

archetypes.title: Inclusion Modification
archetypes.operatorDescription: Aluminum-killed steel always contains alumina inclusions (Al2O3). These are hard, angular particles that cluster together into stringers during rolling, and they are the primary cause of nozzle clogging during continuous casting, surface defects on finished product, and fatigue failures in high-duty applications like bearings and suspension springs. The standard remedy is calcium treatment -- injecting calcium (typically as CaSi wire or CaFe wire) into the ladle to convert the solid alumina inclusions into liquid calcium aluminates (CaO-Al2O3) that are spherical, do not cluster, and float out of the steel more readily.

archetypes.operatorDescription: Temperature is the invisible enemy of ladle metallurgy. A typical heat loses 3-5 degrees C per minute during treatment, and the total temperature drop from tap to cast can be 60-120 degrees C depending on treatment complexity and waiting time.

archetypes.title: Ladle Refractory Management
archetypes.operatorDescription: A ladle fleet at a major steel plant consists of 15-30 ladles, each with a refractory lining that costs $80,000-200,000 to install and lasts 80-150 heats depending on the grade mix and treatment intensity. The lining consists of a working lining (typically MgO-C or Al2O3-MgO-C bricks in the barrel and bottom, high-alumina castable or brick in the slag line) and a permanent lining behind it. The working lining wears from three mechanisms: chemical erosion from the slag (especially high-FeO or high-MnO slag in the slag line zone), thermal cycling (each empty-to-full-to-empty cycle creates thermal stress that spalls the hot face), and mechanical erosion from argon stirring (the plume impingement zone around the porous plugs wears faster than surrounding areas).

archetypes.title: Vacuum Degassing Optimization
archetypes.operatorDescription: Vacuum degassing is essential for producing steel with ultra-low gas content -- hydrogen below 1.5 ppm for heavy plate and forging grades (to avoid flaking and hydrogen-induced cracking), nitrogen below 40 ppm for deep-drawing IF steels and electrical steels, and carbon below 30 ppm for ultra-low-carbon grades processed by RH (Ruhrstahl-Heraeus) vacuum treatment. The two dominant technologies are the RH degasser (where steel circulates between the ladle and a vacuum vessel through two snorkels) and the VD (vacuum degassing in the ladle under a sealed tank lid). Both achieve vacuum levels of 0.5-2 mbar, but the fluid dynamics and therefore the optimization levers are fundamentally different.

archetypes.title: Wire Feeding Optimization
archetypes.operatorDescription: Wire feeding is the precision instrument of ladle metallurgy. While bulk alloy additions (throwing 500 kg of ferromanganese lumps into the ladle) handle the heavy lifting of chemistry adjustment, wire feeding handles the fine work -- calcium treatment (CaSi wire per L2-04-03), precise titanium additions for IF steel (FeTi wire at 1-3 kg Ti/heat where the window is +/- 0.002%), niobium additions for HSLA grades (FeNb wire at 0.5-2 kg Nb/heat), sulfur additions for free-machining grades (FeS wire targeting 0.020-0.035% S), and aluminum adjustments (Al wire for deoxidation trim). You need to decide how many heats to string together in one casting sequence, which grades go in what order, and how to manage the tundish and mold through the whole campaign. A longer sequence means fewer start/stop cycles - each startup and shutdown wastes 30-60 minutes of production time, burns a set of dummy bars and startup scrap, and the first and last heats of a sequence always have degraded quality.

archetypes.title: Nozzle Clogging Prevention
archetypes.operatorDescription: Nozzle clogging is the slow-motion disaster that ruins what should be a good casting sequence. The submerged entry nozzle sits between the tundish and the mold, and over the course of a sequence, alumina and other non-metallic inclusions deposit on the inner wall of the nozzle bore and the port exits. The flow cross-section shrinks, the flow pattern into the mold changes, and eventually the operator has to open the stopper rod or slide gate further and further to maintain the same throughput.

archetypes.title: Strand Surface Temperature Profile Optimization
archetypes.operatorDescription: Every steel grade has a temperature range where the surface ductility drops to near zero - the so-called ductility trough, typically between 700 and 900 degrees C depending on chemistry. If the strand surface passes through that range while it is being bent, straightened, or thermally stressed, you get transverse cracks, corner cracks, or surface hot tears. The whole point of managing the surface temperature profile is to keep the surface either above or below that trough at the critical mechanical deformation points in the machine - the bending zone, the straightening zone, and any areas with high thermal gradient from spray rebound or roller contact.

archetypes.title: Intermix Management
archetypes.operatorDescription: When you transition from one grade to the next within a casting sequence, the steel in the tundish does not change instantaneously. You get a mixing zone where the old grade and the new grade blend together, and that mixed-chemistry steel ends up in slabs that do not fully meet either grade specification. These intermix slabs are the bane of the quality department.

archetypes.title: Reheat Furnace Optimization
archetypes.operatorDescription: The reheat furnace is the biggest energy consumer in the hot strip mill, burning 1-1.5 GJ of natural gas per ton of steel reheated. The job is to bring slabs from ambient or hot-charge temperature up to 1200-1280C (depending on grade) with a uniform temperature through the thickness, minimal scale formation, and enough time at temperature for any microalloying elements to dissolve. Sounds straightforward, but in practice it is a continuous juggling act between energy efficiency, production rate, and metallurgical requirements.

archetypes.title: Rolling Schedule Optimization
archetypes.operatorDescription: The pass schedule is the DNA of the hot strip mill. It defines how a 200-250mm thick slab gets reduced to a 1.5-25mm strip in a series of rolling passes - typically 5-7 passes through the roughing mill to make a 25-45mm transfer bar, then 5-7 stands in the finishing mill to hit the final gauge. Each pass has a draft (how much thickness you take), a speed, and a temperature, and getting the schedule right means hitting the target thickness within +/- 0.5-1.0%, achieving the flatness profile the customer wants, developing the right microstructure for mechanical properties, and doing it all without overloading the motors or breaking a roll.

archetypes.title: Roll Gap and Speed Coordination
archetypes.operatorDescription: In a tandem finishing mill with 5-7 stands running simultaneously, mass flow has to balance perfectly: what comes out of stand F1 has to go into stand F2 at exactly the right speed, and so on down the line. If the speeds do not match, the strip between stands either piles up (creating a loop that can cobble) or gets pulled tight (creating tension that thins the strip and causes width necking). The automatic gauge control (AGC) system adjusts roll gaps in real time based on thickness measurements, and the speed cascade keeps the stands synchronized.

archetypes.title: Cooling Table Optimization
archetypes.operatorDescription: The run-out table is where the hot band gets its final metallurgical identity. The strip comes out of the last finishing stand at 820-920C and passes over a cooling table that is 80-150 meters long, lined with banks of water headers (laminar flow or spray) on top and bottom. The target is to cool the strip from finishing temperature to coiling temperature - anywhere from 450C for bainitic grades to 720C for soft formable grades - at a controlled rate that produces the right microstructure.

archetypes.title: Coiling Temperature Optimization
archetypes.operatorDescription: Coiling temperature is the single most important number on a hot band for many grades, because it determines the final transformation state of the microstructure. The cooling table (L2-06-04) controls the rate of cooling, but the target coiling temperature determines where you stop - what fraction of the transformation is complete when the strip wraps onto the coiler and slow-cools in the coil. For a standard structural grade, you might target 620C to get a fine ferrite-pearlite with good yield strength.

archetypes.title: Roll Wear Prediction and Change Scheduling
archetypes.operatorDescription: Rolls are the most expensive consumable in the hot strip mill, and scheduling when to change them is a constant negotiation between production and quality. Work rolls in the finishing mill last 50-200 km of rolled strip depending on the grade mix and roll material, and as they wear, the roll profile changes - the roll crown flattens out, the surface roughness degrades, and the thermal crown from asymmetric heating shifts. All of this affects strip crown, flatness, and surface quality.

archetypes.title: Width Control Optimization
archetypes.operatorDescription: Width control in the hot strip mill is the ugly stepchild of rolling - everyone talks about gauge and flatness, but width is what determines whether you can ship the coil to the customer or not. If the strip width is 2mm too narrow at any point along the length, the coil fails the specification and either gets downgraded, trimmed at the cold mill (losing yield), or worse, sent to a customer who rejects it. Width is set primarily in the roughing mill by the vertical edger rolls that squeeze the slab edges before each horizontal pass, and then it spreads slightly during each flat pass depending on the draft, friction, and temperature.

archetypes.title: Crown and Flatness Control
archetypes.operatorDescription: Flatness is the hardest thing to get right on a hot strip mill, and it is the first thing the customer complains about. A flat strip means the thickness profile across the width is uniform enough that the strip lies flat on a table without waves, buckles, or camber. The profile is controlled by the roll gap shape, which depends on: the ground roll crown (machined into the roll), thermal crown (from roll heating during rolling), roll wear, roll bending (hydraulic cylinders that flex the roll necks), and on CVC (continuously variable crown) mills, the axial shift position of specially ground rolls that change the effective crown when shifted.

archetypes.title: Hot Band Temperature Uniformity
archetypes.operatorDescription: Temperature uniformity - across the width, along the length, and through the thickness - is the hidden variable behind half of hot rolling quality problems. When the finishing temperature varies by 30-50C from edge to center, the mechanical properties vary by the same proportion. The edge runs cooler because it loses heat from both the top/bottom surfaces and the side, and by the time you are through the finishing mill, the edge might be 40-80C colder than the center on a wide strip.

archetypes.title: Cold Reduction Schedule Optimization
archetypes.operatorDescription: Cold rolling takes the hot band (typically 1.8-6mm thick) and reduces it to final gauge (0.15-3mm) at ambient temperature, which means the steel is work-hardened and the rolling forces are much higher per unit of reduction than in hot rolling. The pass schedule - how you distribute the total reduction across 3-6 stands on a tandem mill or multiple passes on a reversing mill - determines everything: whether you can actually roll the strip without exceeding motor or roll force limits, whether the strip shape and flatness come out right, whether the surface finish meets requirements, and how much energy you burn doing it. On a 5-stand tandem mill, a typical schedule might take 2.5mm hot band down to 0.8mm in reductions of roughly 35%-30%-25%-20%-15% across the five stands.

archetypes.title: Lubrication Optimization
archetypes.operatorDescription: Lubrication in cold rolling is one of those things that does not get enough attention until something goes wrong, and then it is the cause of half your problems. The rolling oil (typically a mineral oil or synthetic ester emulsion at 2-5% concentration in water) does three jobs: it reduces friction in the roll bite to lower rolling forces and energy, it cools the rolls and strip to manage thermal crown, and it protects the strip surface from welding to the roll (which causes heat scratches and surface defects). Getting the balance right between these three functions is the optimization problem, and it is harder than it sounds because they conflict with each other.

archetypes.title: Tension Control Optimization
archetypes.operatorDescription: Tension between stands on a cold tandem mill is the invisible force that holds everything together - literally. archetypes.title: Slitting and Cut-to-Length Optimization
archetypes.operatorDescription: Slitting and cut-to-length (CTL) are the final conversion steps that transform master coils into the widths and sheet lengths customers actually need. A master coil at 1200-1600mm width gets slit into 2-6 narrower strips (mults) that are recoiled, or it gets cut into rectangular sheets at specific lengths. The optimization problem is deceptively simple: given a master coil of known width and a set of customer orders for narrower widths, find the combination of slit widths that maximizes the usable material and minimizes the leftover edge trim waste.

classificationTags: Decision type: allocation (coils to orders), design (cutting patterns)

archetypes.title: Surface Inspection Integration
archetypes.operatorDescription: Surface inspection systems (SIS) are installed on virtually every modern processing line -- hot strip mills, cold mills, coating lines, temper mills -- and they generate enormous amounts of data. A typical system uses high-resolution cameras (4k-8k pixels across the width) running at line speed (up to 1500 m/min on a hot strip mill) and produces images of the top and bottom surface at a resolution of 0.1-0.5mm per pixel. The image processing algorithms detect anomalies -- dark spots, bright spots, scratches, scale residue, roll marks, dross inclusions, coating defects -- and classify them into defect types.

archetypes.title: Painting/Organic Coating Optimization
archetypes.operatorDescription: The paint line (also called a color coating line or coil coating line) applies organic coatings -- primer, topcoat, and sometimes a backing coat -- to galvanized or galvalume steel strip in a continuous process. The strip passes through a chemical pre-treatment section, a primer coater, a prime cure oven, a topcoat coater, a top cure oven, and a cooling section, all at line speeds of 60-180 m/min. The product is pre-painted steel used for building panels, appliances, garage doors, and other applications where the steel arrives at the fabricator ready to form without any further painting.

archetypes.title: Batch Annealing Cycle Optimization
archetypes.operatorDescription: Batch annealing is one of those processes where you are basically flying blind for three to five days. You stack four or five coils on a base, put the inner cover on, seal it, and fire the furnace. The thermocouple readings you get are from the base and maybe one or two spots on the outer cover - you have no direct measurement of what the cold spot in the middle of that coil stack is actually doing.

archetypes.title: Continuous Annealing Furnace Optimization
archetypes.operatorDescription: The continuous annealing line is one of the most complex pieces of equipment in the whole plant - you have got a strip running at 200-600 meters per minute through a heating section, a soaking section, a slow cooling section, a rapid cooling section (gas jet or water quench depending on the line), an overaging section, and a final cooling section. Each zone has its own temperature setpoint, and the line speed ties everything together because it determines how long the strip sits in each zone. Change the speed and every zone thermal profile shifts.

archetypes.operatorDescription: Normalizing is supposed to be the simple heat treatment - heat it above the upper critical, hold it, pull it out and let it air cool. The normalizing furnace runs plates and heavy sections through a roller hearth at a set speed, and the temperature setpoint and residence time have to be matched to the thickness and the grade.

archetypes.operatorDescription: Quench and temper is where you really earn your money in plate and bar production. You are austenitizing the steel, quenching it hard - water, polymer, or oil depending on the product - and then tempering it back to get the combination of strength and toughness the customer needs. The problem is that quenching is violent.

archetypes.title: Stress Relieving Optimization
archetypes.operatorDescription: Stress relieving is the treatment nobody wants to pay for but everybody needs when something distorts during machining or fails in service from hydrogen cracking. You take a welded fabrication or a heavy plate that has been flame-cut and you soak it at 550-680C for an hour or more per inch of thickness, then slow-cool it. The point is to relax the residual stresses from welding, rolling, or quenching without changing the microstructure or the mechanical properties.

archetypes.operatorDescription: Every time you change grades during a casting sequence, you create an intermix zone in the strand where the chemistry is transitioning from one grade to the next. The tundish acts as a mixing vessel - you stop pouring the old ladle, start pouring the new ladle with different chemistry, and for some number of tons the steel in the tundish is a blend of old and new. That intermix material has to go somewhere.

archetypes.title: Product Certification Optimization
archetypes.operatorDescription: Certification is the last gate before material ships, and it is where all the process variability and testing uncertainty funnel into a binary decision: does this piece meet the spec or not? The quality engineer looks at the chemistry, the mechanical test results, the dimensional measurements, and the inspection reports, checks them all against the customer order specification and the applicable standard (ASTM, EN, API, whatever), and either releases the material or holds it. The problem is that this process is manual, slow, and either too conservative or too risky depending on who is doing it.

archetypes.title: Statistical Process Control Optimization
archetypes.operatorDescription: SPC is one of those things every steel plant says they do, but most do badly. You have control charts on the HMI screens for temperature, chemistry, dimensions, whatever - and the control limits were set five years ago based on data from a different product mix with different raw materials. The operators see the charts, but the alarms fire so often that nobody pays attention anymore.
archetypes.timeToValue: Phase 1 (Months 1-4): Infrastructure and Baseline**
classificationTags: Decision type: design | diagnosis

Uncertainty structure: stochastic-known (process variability models from historical data)
Constraint class: quality, capacity (operator attention as a scarce resource)
archetypes.mathematicalDescription: SPC optimization is a joint design problem spanning control chart parameter selection, alarm system architecture, and monitoring network configuration. For each monitored variable X_j, the classical formulation selects control limits (mu_j +/- k * sigma_j), sampling interval h_j, and sample size n_j to minimize a cost function: E[C] = C_false_alarm * ARL_0^{-1} + C_missed_detection * integral(ARL_1(delta) * f(delta) d(delta)) + C_sampling * n_j / h_j, where ARL_0 is the in-control average run length (inversely proportional to false alarm rate), ARL_1(delta) is the out-of-control average run length for a shift of size delta, and f(delta) is the distribution of shift magnitudes.

archetypes.title: Predictive Maintenance Scheduling
archetypes.operatorDescription: The maintenance department is always caught between two bad outcomes: fix it too early and you waste parts and labor on equipment that had life left in it, or fix it too late and you get an unplanned breakdown that shuts down a production line for eight hours during peak demand. The traditional approach is time-based PM - change the bearing every 6,000 hours, reline the furnace every 18 months, rebuild the hydraulic cylinder every year - regardless of actual condition. Everybody knows this is wasteful because some bearings last 12,000 hours and some fail at 3,000, but the calendar-based schedule is easy to plan around and nobody gets fired for following the PM schedule.

On the other hand, when the main mill drive coupling fails at 2 AM on a Sunday, and the only spare is a 16-week lead time item from Germany, the plant manager wants to know why we did not have one on the shelf.

archetypes.mathematicalDescription: Spare parts inventory optimization is a multi-item stochastic inventory control problem with heterogeneous demand patterns and criticality-dependent service level targets. archetypes.title: Maintenance-Production Co-Optimization
archetypes.operatorDescription: In most steel plants, maintenance and production planning are done by two separate departments that barely talk to each other. Production planning says "we need the hot strip mill running 24/7 for the next three weeks to fill the order book." Maintenance says "we need the hot strip mill down for 12 hours to replace a gearbox coupling that is showing vibration." Neither side has a framework for evaluating the trade-off - is the coupling replacement worth $600,000 in lost production, or is the risk of a catastrophic failure worth the continued operation? The answer depends on the failure probability curve, the production value at stake, and what alternative production paths exist, but nobody has those numbers in a form that supports the decision.

archetypes.title: Reliability-Centered Maintenance Strategy
archetypes.operatorDescription: RCM is supposed to answer the question "what is the right maintenance strategy for each piece of equipment?" but in most plants, the RCM analysis was done once by consultants, produced a 500-page report, and now sits on a shelf collecting dust. The report said things like "apply condition-based maintenance to the main drive gearbox" and "run-to-failure is acceptable for non-critical conveyor idlers" - which everyone already knew. The value of RCM is in the systematic failure mode analysis that identifies which failure modes are age-related (and therefore candidates for time-based replacement), which are condition-related (candidates for monitoring), and which are random (where no amount of PM helps and you just need redundancy or rapid repair capability).

archetypes.title: Melt Shop to Caster Coordination
archetypes.operatorDescription: The melt shop-to-caster handoff is the tightest coordination problem in the entire steel plant, and getting it wrong costs you immediately. A heat of steel in a ladle is a ticking clock - from tap to the start of casting, you have maybe 30-60 minutes before the steel temperature drops below castable range, the ladle refractory degrades past the point where you can hold it, and the inclusion chemistry evolves to where it will clog the tundish nozzle. Every minute of delay in that window is a problem, and if you miss the window entirely, you either reline the ladle and retap (if the steel is still in the furnace), dump the heat (catastrophic loss of $50-100K), or force-cast with marginal temperature and accept the quality hit.
archetypes.timeToValue: Phase 1 (4-6 months): Real-time visibility dashboard showing ladle locations, temperatures, predicted timing - value from improved situational awareness ($0.2-0.5M/year in avoided coordination failure
classificationTags: Decision type: scheduling | sequencing | allocation
Time horizon: operational (minutes-hours) for real-time coordination; tactical (days-weeks) for sequence planning
Objective structure: bi-objective (caster utilization vs. temperature/quality margin)
Uncertainty structure: stochastic-known (process time distributions, ladle thermal models with measured parameters)
Constraint class: capacity, physical-limits, quality, safety, logical
archetypes.mathematicalDescription: Formulate as a hybrid flow-shop scheduling and resource allocation problem with timing synchronization constraints. Decision variables include: heat start times at each stage (EAF/BOF, LMF, caster), ladle-to-heat assignments, tundish change timing within casting sequences, and buffer time allocations between stages.
crossIndustryAnalogs: Semiconductor Wafer Fab - Furnace Bay Coordination
equipmentVariants: Single-EAF, Single-Caster (1-1.5M tons/year)
Dual-EAF or BOF, Dual-Caster (2-3M tons/year)

archetypes.title: Caster to Hot Mill Coordination
archetypes.operatorDescription: The interface between the caster and the hot mill is where you either save a fortune on energy or waste it, depending on how well the two operations are synchronized. A slab comes off the caster at 800-1000 degrees C. If you can charge it directly into the reheat furnace within 20-60 minutes (direct hot charging, DHC), you save $8-15/ton in reheating fuel because you are starting with an 800-degree slab instead of an ambient-temperature one.
archetypes.timeToValue: Phase 1 (3-6 months): Slab tracking and DHC rate monitoring dashboard - value from visibility and measurement ($0.3-0.8M/year from improved manual DHC decisions with better information)
classificationTags: Decision type: sequencing | scheduling
Time horizon: tactical (days-weeks) for sequence alignment planning; operational (minutes-hours) for real-time DHC decisions
Objective structure: bi-objective (maximize DHC energy savings vs. minimize sequence transition penalties)
Uncertainty structure: stochastic-known (caster and mill delay distributions, slab temperature loss models)
Constraint class: quality, capacity, physical-limits, logical
archetypes.mathematicalDescription: Formulate as a coupled sequencing and timing synchronization problem. Decision variables include: casting sequence order (constrained by grade/width transition rules), rolling sequence order (constrained by width/gauge transition rules), direct-hot-charge assignment d_s (binary, for each slab s), and slab-to-furnace charging timing.
equipmentVariants: Integrated Mill with Walking-Beam Furnaces (2-3M tons/year)
Compact Strip Mill / Thin-Slab Caster (0.5-2M tons/year)
Multi-Caster, Multi-Furnace Complex (3-5M tons/year)

archetypes.title: Hot Mill to Cold Mill/Finishing Coordination
archetypes.operatorDescription: The transition from the hot mill to downstream processing - cold rolling, pickling, annealing, galvanizing, temper rolling, inspection - is where the product really gets customized, and the scheduling complexity explodes. A single hot-rolled coil might go through 3-6 additional process steps depending on the final product: pickle, cold roll, anneal, temper, galvanize, inspect, slit. Each of those steps runs on different equipment with different capacity, different setup characteristics, and different queue behavior.
archetypes.timeToValue: Phase 1 (4-8 months): WIP visibility dashboard with buffer level tracking, aging alerts, and flow time measurement - value from awareness and manual optimization ($0.3-1.0M/year)
classificationTags: Decision type: scheduling | routing | allocation
Time horizon: operational (minutes-hours) for line-level scheduling; tactical (days-weeks) for intermediate inventory positioning
Objective structure: multi-objective (minimize flow time, maximize line utilization, minimize WIP)
Uncertainty structure: stochastic-known (line uptimes, processing time variability, quality yields)
Constraint class: capacity, quality, physical-limits, contractual, logical
archetypes.mathematicalDescription: Formulate as a multi-stage flexible flow-shop scheduling problem with intermediate inventory management. Decision variables include: coil-to-line assignment for each process stage (when alternatives exist), processing sequence at each line, and release timing between stages (determining intermediate buffer levels).
equipmentVariants: Integrated Flat-Product Mill (2-3M tons/year, pickle + cold mill + galvanizing + temper)

archetypes.title: Real-Time Rescheduling Under Disruption
archetypes.operatorDescription: No plan survives contact with reality in a steel mill. You build a beautiful weekly schedule, and then on Tuesday the hot mill has a cobble that takes out three hours of rolling, or the EAF trips on a water leak and you lose two heats, or the biggest customer calls and says they need their order a week early because their customer moved their shutdown. Now the scheduler has to figure out, in real time and under pressure, how to recover.
archetypes.timeToValue: Phase 1 (3-4 months)**: Disruption detection and classification system. Automated disruption event logging and repair time tracking. Value: improved disruption data quality for future optimization.
classificationTags: Decision type: scheduling | sequencing | switching
Time horizon: real-time (<60s) for immediate response; operational (minutes-hours) for full reschedule
Objective structure: multi-objective (minimize total delay, minimize schedule nervousness, minimize cost)
Uncertainty structure: robust (unknown repair durations) with stochastic-known elements (historical disruption patterns)
Constraint class: capacity, quality, contractual, logical, physical-limits, safety
archetypes.mathematicalDescription: Formulate as a dynamic rescheduling problem with the current state as initial condition. Given a disruption event (equipment failure with estimated repair time, quality diversion of specific material, new rush order with hard deadline), the decision variables are the modified schedule: revised sequence and timing for all operations at all affected process stages, including order re-prioritization, lot reassignment, and process route changes.
equipmentVariants: Integrated Mill (BF-BOF route, 2-5M ton/year)
EAF Mini-Mill (0.5-1.5M ton/year)
Specialty/Stainless Mill (0.2-0.8M ton/year)

archetypes.title: Multi-Product Campaign Sequencing
archetypes.operatorDescription: Steel plants do not produce one product at a time - they produce families of products in campaigns, and the order in which you run those campaigns determines how much production time you lose to transitions. At the caster, you group heats into sequences by grade family and width because changing grades mid-sequence means a tundish change (5-15 minutes of lost casting time) and changing widths means adjusting the mold (another 5-10 minutes). At the hot mill, you run width campaigns from wide to narrow within a work roll set because going narrow-to-wide creates poor shape from differential roll wear.
archetypes.timeToValue: Phase 1 (2-3 months)**: Transition cost model calibration and campaign performance dashboard. Data-driven visibility into actual campaign transition costs vs. historical assumptions. Value: identifies
classificationTags: Decision type: sequencing | scheduling
Time horizon: tactical (days-weeks) for campaign planning; operational (minutes-hours) for within-campaign sequencing
Objective structure: multi-objective (minimize transition losses, minimize inventory, maximize on-time delivery)
Uncertainty structure: stochastic-known (demand forecasts, process time variability) with robust elements (minimum campaign feasibility margins)
Constraint class: quality, capacity, physical-limits, contractual, logical
archetypes.mathematicalDescription: Formulate as a joint campaign length and sequence optimization problem. Decision variables include: campaign composition C_k (set of products in campaign k), campaign length L_k (number of heats, tons, or hours), campaign sequence order pi (permutation of campaigns within a planning horizon), and within-campaign product sequencing.
crossIndustryAnalogs: Semiconductor Manufacturing (Wafer Fab Campaign / Lot Grouping)
equipmentVariants: Integrated Mill (BF-BOF, 2-5M ton/year, flat products)
EAF Mini-Mill (0.5-1.5M ton/year, long products)
Specialty/Stainless Mill (0.2-0.8M ton/year)

archetypes.title: Bottleneck Identification and Dynamic Capacity Allocation
archetypes.operatorDescription: Ask three different people in a steel mill what the bottleneck is, and you will get three different answers - and they might all be right at different times of the week. Monday morning when the hot mill is rolling a thick-gauge campaign at low speed, the hot mill is the bottleneck and the melt shop is backing up slabs into the yard. Tuesday afternoon when the mill switches to thin gauge and the rolling speed doubles, suddenly the melt shop cannot keep up and the reheat furnace has gaps.
archetypes.timeToValue: Phase 1 (2-3 months)**: Bottleneck detection dashboard. Real-time visualization of production rates, buffer levels, and current bottleneck indicator. No resource allocation optimization yet. Value: aw
classificationTags: Decision type: allocation | diagnosis
Time horizon: real-time (<60s) for bottleneck identification; operational (minutes-hours) for resource reallocation; tactical (days-weeks) for staffing and maintenance planning
Objective structure: single (maximize plant throughput subject to resource constraints)
Uncertainty structure: stochastic-known (product mix forecasts, equipment reliability distributions)
Constraint class: capacity, physical-limits, logical
archetypes.mathematicalDescription: Formulate as a dynamic bottleneck detection and resource allocation problem. The detection layer is an online estimation problem: given real-time production rates, buffer levels, and equipment states across all process stages, identify the current binding constraint.
crossIndustryAnalogs: Highway Traffic Management (Dynamic Bottleneck and Ramp Metering)
equipmentVariants: Integrated Mill (BF-BOF, 2-5M ton/year)
EAF Mini-Mill (0.5-1.5M ton/year)

archetypes.title: Order-to-Delivery Lead Time Optimization
archetypes.operatorDescription: Lead time is the metric that customers care about most after price and quality, and it is the one that most steel plants manage the worst. A customer places an order and gets told "4-6 weeks" - that range itself is a sign of the problem. The actual manufacturing time for a coil of steel through the entire process chain is maybe 3-5 days of processing time.
archetypes.timeToValue: Phase 1 (2-4 months)**: Lead time prediction model. ML-based flow time prediction deployed as a reporting/analytics tool. Compares predicted vs. quoted lead times. Value: identifies orders at risk of
classificationTags: Decision type: routing | scheduling | allocation
Time horizon: operational (minutes-hours) for priority management; tactical (days-weeks) for route selection and lead time quoting
Objective structure: bi-objective (minimize flow time vs. maximize lead time prediction accuracy)
Uncertainty structure: stochastic-known (processing time distributions, disruption probabilities) with robust elements (lead time guarantee under worst-case scenarios)
Constraint class: capacity, contractual, logical, quality
archetypes.mathematicalDescription: Formulate as a joint routing, priority, and lead-time estimation problem. Decision variables include: process route selection r_o for each order o from the set of feasible routes, priority score p_o for sequencing across shared resources, and quoted lead time Q_o.
crossIndustryAnalogs: Healthcare (Patient Appointment Scheduling and Wait Time Management)
equipmentVariants: Integrated Mill (BF-BOF, 2-5M ton/year, flat products)
EAF Mini-Mill (0.5-1.5M ton/year)
Specialty/Stainless (0.2-0.8M ton/year)

archetypes.title: Scrap Supplier Optimization
archetypes.operatorDescription: Every EAF shop buys scrap from a portfolio of suppliers, and the procurement team walks a tightrope between cost, quality, and reliability. You might have 20-50 active scrap suppliers ranging from large national brokers to small local yards, each with different pricing, different quality profiles, different delivery reliability, and different volume capacity. The cheapest supplier might deliver shredded scrap at $320/ton but with copper running 0.18-0.25% and delivery windows that slip by 2-3 days regularly.
archetypes.timeToValue: +--> [Weekly Allocation Plan] --> [ERP Purchase Orders]
classificationTags: Decision type: allocation | blending
Time horizon: tactical (days-weeks) for allocation; strategic (months+) for contract negotiation
Objective structure: multi-objective (minimize total cost, minimize quality risk, maximize supply reliability)
Uncertainty structure: stochastic-known (supplier quality distributions from inspection data, price forecasts from market models)
Constraint class: contractual, capacity, quality, physical-limits
archetypes.mathematicalDescription: Formulate as a multi-supplier allocation problem with quality uncertainty. Decision variables include volume allocation q_i to each supplier i for each scrap grade g over a planning period, spot market purchase quantities q_spot(t), and contract structure parameters (commitment levels, price ceilings, quality guarantees) for upcoming negotiations.
equipmentVariants: G.1 Small EAF Mini-Mill (< 500 kt/year)
G.2 Medium EAF Mill (500 kt - 1.5 Mt/year)
G.3 Large Multi-Source Operation (> 1.5 Mt/year)

archetypes.title: Alloy and Consumable Procurement
archetypes.operatorDescription: A steel mill consumes dozens of alloys, fluxes, refractories, and consumables, and running out of any one of them can shut down production or force expensive substitutions. Ferromanganese, ferrosilicon, ferrochromium, aluminum wire, calcium-silicon cored wire, lime, dolomite, fluorspar, mold powder, SEN (submerged entry nozzle) assemblies, tundish linings, ladle bricks - the list goes on. Each has different pricing dynamics, different lead times (some are two-day domestic orders, others are six-week imports from South Africa or China), different shelf-life considerations, and different consumption patterns that depend on the production mix.
archetypes.timeToValue: Demand forecasting: Python scikit-learn/XGBoost for per-item models. Retrain weekly; inference per heat < 100 ms.
classificationTags: Decision type: scheduling | allocation
Time horizon: operational (minutes-hours) for emergency reorders; tactical (days-weeks) for regular procurement; strategic (months+) for annual contracts and hedging
Objective structure: bi-objective (minimize procurement cost vs. minimize stockout risk)
Uncertainty structure: stochastic-known (demand from production models, price from market models) with robust elements (minimum safety stock under worst-case demand)
Constraint class: capacity, contractual, physical-limits
archetypes.mathematicalDescription: Formulate as a multi-item inventory management and procurement optimization problem under price and demand uncertainty. Decision variables include order quantities q_j(t) and order timing for each consumable j, supplier selection s_j(t) when multiple suppliers exist, and safety stock levels SS_j.
equipmentVariants: G.1 Small EAF Mini-Mill (< 500 kt/year)
G.2 Medium EAF Mill (500 kt - 1.5 Mt/year)
G.3 Large Integrated or Multi-Mill Operation (> 1.5 Mt/year)

archetypes.title: Customer Order Acceptance Optimization
archetypes.operatorDescription: Every order that comes through the door looks like revenue, but not every order is good for the plant. The sales team wants to say yes to everything because their commission is on tons sold, not on plant efficiency. But the production planning team knows that accepting a small order of an unusual grade forces a special campaign at the caster, wastes transition time at the hot mill, ties up the finishing line for a product that does not fill a full coil, and pushes back regular production.
archetypes.timeToValue: Weekly bid-price update: 10-30 minutes (Monte Carlo simulation of order arrivals).
classificationTags: Decision type: allocation | switching
Time horizon: operational (minutes-hours) for individual order decisions; tactical (days-weeks) for order book management
Objective structure: single (maximize total portfolio contribution margin)
Uncertainty structure: stochastic-known (future order arrival distributions from demand forecasts, production time variability)
Constraint class: capacity, contractual, quality, logical
archetypes.mathematicalDescription: Formulate as a dynamic order acceptance and pricing problem. For each incoming order o with attributes (grade, dimensions, quantity, requested due date, offered price), the decision variables are: accept/reject decision a_o (binary), quoted price p_o (if negotiable), and promised delivery date D_o.
equipmentVariants: G.1 Commodity Steel Mill (Simple Product Mix)
G.2 Mixed Product Mill (Moderate Complexity)
G.3 Specialty / Automotive-Grade Mill (High Complexity)

archetypes.title: Product Mix Optimization
archetypes.operatorDescription: The product mix decision is the highest-leverage strategic question in a steel mill: given limited capacity and a range of products you could sell at different prices, which products should you make? A plant that can produce commodity hot-rolled coil at $600/ton or automotive-grade galvanized at $900/ton obviously wants to produce the high-value product - but the automotive grade consumes more capacity (slower casting, tighter hot mill practice, extra cold rolling and galvanizing passes), requires more expensive raw materials (cleaner scrap, more alloy), has higher quality rejection rates, and demands more process capability. The net margin per ton may be higher on automotive but the margin per constraint-hour might actually be lower, and if the constraint is the hot mill, you make more total profit running commodity product faster.
archetypes.timeToValue: Phase 1 (Months 1-3)**: Data assembly and LP formulation. Build capacity model, variable cost model, and initial demand/price forecasts. Validate LP solution against recent historical performance.
classificationTags: Decision type: allocation | blending
Time horizon: tactical (days-weeks) for rolling mix adjustment; strategic (months+) for annual product-mix planning
Objective structure: single (maximize total contribution margin) or bi-objective (margin vs. market share/customer retention)
Uncertainty structure: stochastic-known (price forecasts, demand distributions) with robust elements (minimum margin under worst-case price scenarios)
Constraint class: capacity, contractual, quality, physical-limits
archetypes.mathematicalDescription: Formulate as a multi-period product-mix linear (or mixed-integer) program. Decision variables include production volume x_p for each product p in each period t, capacity allocation by process stage, and raw material procurement quantities.
equipmentVariants: G.1 Commodity-Focused Mill (HRC/Plate/Rebar)
G.2 Mixed Product Mill (HRC + CRC + Coated)
G.3 Specialty / Automotive-Focused Mill

archetypes.title: Multi-Plant Production Allocation
archetypes.operatorDescription: When a steel company operates two or more mills, every customer order triggers a question: which plant should make this? On the surface it seems simple - send the order to the plant closest to the customer to minimize freight, or to the plant with the best capability for that product. But the real tradeoffs are much deeper.
archetypes.timeToValue: Weekly full re-optimization with stochastic scenarios: 10-30 minutes.
classificationTags: Decision type: allocation | routing
Time horizon: tactical (days-weeks) for order allocation; strategic (months+) for capacity investment and capability planning
Objective structure: single (maximize company-wide contribution margin) or bi-objective (margin vs. plant utilization balance)
Uncertainty structure: stochastic-known (demand forecasts, freight rate variability) with robust elements (minimum utilization guarantees)
Constraint class: capacity, contractual, logical, physical-limits
archetypes.mathematicalDescription: Formulate as a multi-facility production allocation and inter-plant logistics problem. Decision variables include: order-to-plant assignment z_{op} (binary or fractional, allowing split orders across plants), inter-plant material transfer quantities f_{p1,p2,product}(t), and capacity utilization targets by plant and process stage.
equipmentVariants: G.1 Two-Plant Company (Regional)
G.2 Multi-Plant Company (3-5 Plants, National)
G.3 Multi-National or Multi-Division Company (5+ Plants)

archetypes.title: Demand Forecasting and Inventory Positioning
archetypes.operatorDescription: Steel is a make-to-order business for most products, but the lead times are long enough that you need to anticipate demand and pre-position inventory at various stages of the process to meet customer delivery expectations. Nobody can wait 4-6 weeks for a coil of commodity hot-rolled - the service centers want it off the shelf in 3-5 days, and if you do not have it, they call your competitor. So you end up making some product to forecast, building finished goods inventory of fast-moving items, and maintaining work-in-process inventory of intermediates (hot-rolled coils waiting for cold rolling, cold-rolled waiting for galvanizing) that can be pulled through to customer specs with shorter lead time.
archetypes.timeToValue: Demand forecasting (weekly batch): 5-30 minutes for full product catalog (100-500 products). Uses Python (statsmodels, Prophet, PyTorch for TFT/DeepAR).
classificationTags: Decision type: allocation | design
Time horizon: tactical (days-weeks) for replenishment decisions; strategic (months+) for stocking policy and MTS/MTO boundary design
Objective structure: bi-objective (minimize inventory investment vs. maximize service level)
Uncertainty structure: stochastic-known (demand distributions from forecasting models, lead time variability from production data)
Constraint class: capacity, contractual, physical-limits
archetypes.mathematicalDescription: Formulate as a multi-echelon inventory optimization problem coupled with demand forecasting. The inventory system spans multiple stages: raw materials (scrap, alloys), work-in-process at each process stage (slabs, hot-rolled coils, cold-rolled coils), and finished goods by product family.
crossIndustryAnalogs: Consumer Packaged Goods (CPG) Demand Forecasting and Inventory
equipmentVariants: G.1 Make-to-Order Dominant Mill (Long Products, Plate, Specialty)
G.2 Mixed MTS/MTO Mill (Flat Products, Service Center + Contract)
G.3 Service-Center-Focused Mill (Commodity Flat Products)
